hello.note: Traditional call-out greeting; the customary reply is Rampés. Register note: entries below default to warm-polite (lemes) forms over blunt casual (loma) ones, noted where both are common.

good_evening.note: From dusk onward; the afternoon greeting is wilujeng siang.

goodbye.note: Said to the person leaving, wishing them a safe trip; dugi kapendak deui ('until we meet again') is another common farewell.

how_are_you.note: Kumaha kabarna? (lit. 'how's the news') is another common way to ask.

thank_you.note: Polite (lemes) form; nuhun alone is the everyday casual version.

youre_welcome.note: 'Same to you' (cf. Indonesian sama-sama); listed first among replies to thanks on Omniglot's native-sourced phrase list. Sawangsulna ('in return/likewise') is the other common reply and is what Google Translate maps 'you're welcome' to directly, but sami-sami is the plainer, higher-frequency form, so it leads here.

no_problem.note: Casual 'it's nothing'; round-trips cleanly through Google Translate both directions. Teu kunanaon ('it's okay') is a fuller variant that Google Translate's dictionary (score 10) maps most confidently, so it is a solid alternative if a fuller phrase is wanted; henteu masalah is a more literal, calque-like 'no problem' also attested by Google Translate.

please.note: Multi-purpose politeness word; also used for 'go ahead' or 'here you are'.

excuse_me.note: Permisi/parmisi is a common alternative, especially when passing by.

yes.note: Polite (lemes) form; enya is the everyday casual (loma) form.

no.note: Neutral all-purpose 'no'; teu is the clipped casual form.

of_course.note: Polite (lemes) form; tangtu is the everyday casual root, independently attested on Wiktionary as 'certain, definite, sure'. Google Translate confirms both directions: su→en 'tangtos' gives 'Of course', and en→su 'of course (casual)' gives 'tangtu (kasual)', so the lemes/loma pairing checks out even though no independent phrasebook source was found.

amazing.note: Literally 'very good' (sae round-trips cleanly to 'good' both directions on Google Translate); a general admiration exclamation for food, work, or situations. Éndah pisan ('very beautiful') round-trips to 'very amazing' su→en on Google Translate too, so it works for this sense as well, but is used mainly for scenery and views.

delicious.note: Independently confirmed on Wiktionary as 'delicious' (also 'to feel/taste'); ngeunah is a common synonym for tasty food.

cheers.note: 'May you be healthy'; matches Omniglot's native-sourced 'Mugi sing séhat' for toasts almost exactly (Mugi dipasihan kaséhatan is the more formal variant listed there). Toasting before drinking isn't a strong local tradition.
